thread.title: A top- and bottom-line beat loaded with record holiday quart

author: D.M. Martins Research
title: A top- and bottom-line beat loaded with record holiday quart
text:
A top- and bottom-line beat loaded with record holiday quarter numbers, coupled with lower-than-consensus iPhone units sold and next quarter guidance that lagged Street's estimates. This was Apple's ( AAPL ) fiscal 1Q18 earnings report in a nutshell that, despite far from weak, failed to excite investors as the stock dipped -4% on Friday. 

Image credit 
At the heart of the initial mildly bearish reaction, in my view, was the performance of the iPhone. Apple delivered solid unit sales numbers on a per-week basis (to account for the shorter quarter) and outstanding ASP, propelled by the success of the iPhone X in the model's first few weeks of existence. In fact, the YOY growth in both metrics was the best of the past five quarters at least. The chart below helps to illustrate. 

Source: DM Martins Research, using data from company reports
However, it looks like the Street and more bullish investors had been looking for signs that the so-called iPhone "super cycle" could send smartphone and total company revenues through the roof. Supporting the hopes was a completely redesigned high-end device that would encourage owners of the three-year old iPhone 6 (Apple's critically acclaimed and best-selling device ever) and other models to come out in droves and swap their equipment for the "shiny new thing."
That did not seem to have happened. Or, to be more precise, the apparent initial success of the iPhone X appears to have come along decreased demand for other models, including the new iPhone 8 and 8 Plus. The device activation data that I shared early last week, which I think served as a great indicator of the iPhone sales mix in fiscal 1Q18, provides a good visual.

Source: DM Martins Research, using data from Mixpanel 
To be fair, CEO Tim Cook and team never promised a "super cycle" - or have ever even used the term to communicate the company's vision, to the best of my knowledge. So holding Apple's management accountable for not exceeding other people's expectations sounds unreasonable. But what drives stock prices, at least in the short term, are investors' expectations for future results. And to that regard, it is possible that part of Apple's robust stock price reaction in 2017 (up 46%) might have been in anticipation of the potential "super cycle" that now seems at risk of not materializing. The graph below illustrates how fiscal 2Q18 estimates have come down by quite a bit since the start of 2018.

Source: DM Martins Research using image from YCharts
What to make of it? When it comes to investing in AAPL, there seems to be two ways to think about the matter today: (1) the company is firing on all cylinders and should continue to do well in the foreseeable future, and (2) the so-called iPhone "super cycle" has sputtered and may prove not to be the catalyst for further stock strength in 2018. I happen to believe that both are true.
While I think that "super cycle" believers might choose to exit their positions and perhaps put pressure on the stock in the short term, I remain comfortable in my belief that the company is well positioned to deliver shareholder value over time. It is worth noting that the global economy continues to show signs of strength, and that Apple should be able to operate very well in an environment of robust discretionary spending. Specific to the company itself, Apple is likely to benefit from (1) an ecosystem that continues to grow to support service and accessory sales, (2) a long-awaited rebound in its large mainland China market, and (3) a freed-up pile of cash that could turn into higher dividends, share repurchases or capital investments, only to name a few tailwinds.
In the end and judging by the early read compared to initial Street expectations, the iPhone "super cycle" could be in trouble. But it would be a stretch to think that the company is.
